draft.title: Local politics
card: Pompeii and Herculaneum were Roman towns with their own local officials. Pompeii's magistrates included duoviri, who were the two senior officials, and aediles, who looked after public buildings, streets and markets.
Candidates advertised on walls. Painted notices, called dipinti, were written in red or black paint on house fronts and tomb walls, often by professional sign writers.

A typical notice names the candidate and the office he sought, and asks the public to vote for him. Many also name the supporter who paid for it or backed him, such as a neighbour, a trade group or a shop owner.
Historians use the notices as evidence. They show which offices existed and who sought them. They also show who backed which candidate, though they do not tell us the results of the elections.
draft.remember: Election notices show who stood for office and who backed them, not who won.

a.q: What can historians learn directly from a painted election notice in Pompeii?
opts: Which candidate was asked for and who backed him
Which candidate won the election that year
How many people voted in the election
Which candidate the town's women preferred
a.why: A notice names the candidate, the office and often a supporter. It was painted before the vote, so it cannot show who won. Winning is the most tempting wrong option, but the notices give no results.
a.clue: The notices were painted before people voted.

b.q: A wall in Pompeii reads: 'The bakers ask you to make Gaius aedile.' What does this notice best show?
opts: A trade group publicly backed a candidate for office
Gaius was elected aedile by the bakers
Bakers held the senior offices in the town
Gaius was a baker who ran his own shop
b.why: The notice shows a group of bakers asking for votes for Gaius, so it records support. It does not say he won, and it does not say he was a baker. The tempting option is that he was elected, but a request for votes is not a result.
b.clue: The bakers are asking, not announcing.

a.best: Which candidate was asked for and who backed him

b.best: A trade group publicly backed a candidate for office
